newsitem.title: GERMANY: Djindjic urges West to give aid to Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Djindjic urges West to give aid to Serbia.

text.p: Belgrade Mayor Zoran Djindjic on Tuesday called on western governments for aid to support his fledgling democracy in Serbia and warned there could be a return to bloodshed or dictatorship if reforms did not succeed.

Djindjic, one of Serbia's leading opposition leaders, was on a three-day visit to Germany where he met Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel for talks about the situation in Serbia and to discuss progress on implementing democratic reforms there.

Kinkel urged him and his three-party opposition "Zajedno" (Together) coalition to guarantee press freedoms and protect minority rights particularly those of ethnic Albanians in Kosovo province now that they were in power in some regions.

Speaking at the Friedrich Ebert Foundation in Bonn, Djindjic said Zajedno was committed to democracy but that Serbia was going through an economic crisis and urgently needed aid from the West to fend off the threat of extremism.

"We need support from abroad," he told an audience at the foundation in Bonn. He described how he had toured European cities and asked mayors to donate buses to the bankrupt public transport system in the Serbian capital.
"If we have not succeeded (in implementing reform) by 1999 we can be sure the communists will be back," Djindjic said.
Djindjic took office in February after months of street protests forced Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to recognise Zajedno's local election victory.

When asked if he would be willing to bring extreme nationalist parties or communists into his coalition in order to create a majority, Djindjic said he might, if necessary, integrate their issues into his platform.
"In Serbia, one cannot shut out other parties," he said, speaking in fluent German.
"The majority of us are in the centre (of the political spectrum)," he said, adding that this did not mean Zajedno could not introduce issues from other parties to their platform.

Djindjic said radical right and left-wing parties had the support of 10 to 15 percent of the Serbian electorate, but that if the economy picked up there would be little danger of one of these parties dominating.
